newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania polls favour Iliescu, not his party.
newsitem.headline: Romania polls favour Iliescu, not his party.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu retained his lead in an opinion poll published on Monday two weeks before general elections but his party trailed its main opponents and was even bounced into third place in anothe survey.

A poll in the daily Adevarul gave Iliescu, who has run Romania since the end of communism in 1989, 31.9 percent of voting intentions -- well short of the 50 percent needed for an outright first-round win on November 3.

Second in the field of 16 with 27.2 percent was academic Emil Constantinescu, who finished a distant second to Iliescu in the 1992 election. Romania's first post-communist prime minister, Petre Roman, was third on 21.9 percent.
Constantinescu, who heads the Democratic Convention (CDR) grouping about 15 parties, told the Rompres news agency that he would beat Iliescu in the mid-November run-off.
"The final round when we have our television debate I will win against President Iliescu with a minimum of words going straight to the point," he said.
"But that won't make matters any easier. Romania now is more difficult to govern than the United States."

Constantinescu and Roman say Iliescu has plunged Romania's 23 million people into poverty and is a hold-over from the communist machinery that kept dictator Nicolae Ceausescu in power for more than two decades.
Polls are notoriously unreliable in predominantly rural Romania. Most surveys have put Iliescu in front, but one last week had him trailing both of his main opponents.

In the parliamentary vote, the Adevarul survey, conducted by the IMAS institute, gave Constantinescu's CDR 31.2 percent. The president's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) had 28.5 percent and Roman's Social Democrats (USD) 19.7 percent.

A poll in the daily Romania Libera, asking voters which party they trusted most, put the ruling PDSR in third place for the first time, with 23.5 percent. The CDR led with 35.6 percent followed by the USD on 25.3 percent.
Despite widespread apathy among voters more concerned with economic survival, the campaign has swathed Bucharest streets in posters and generated lively television discussions.

The opposition said the PDSR was conducting fake opinion polls with leading questions to favour Iliescu and a leading member of the European Parliament accused him outright of trying to rig the outcome.
